data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002 requires that panel disagreement predict incorrectness, but for checklist-driven panels this signal is only informative conditional on the checklist mapping being imperfect. Under the exact problem setting (explicit checklist, verifiable outcomes), a well-designed checklist induces a deterministic or near-deterministic item→answer mapping; panel disagreement then reflects rater noise (attention, training variance), not task-relevant uncertainty. SRC_002's own countercondition concedes this: 'The checklist forces a binary choice on each item, eliminating the possibility of calibrated redundancy.' Since explicit checklists for verifiable-outcome tasks typically do force discrete feature→decision steps, the central diagnostic is undefined for the paradigmatic case. Worse, SRC_002 offers no within-evaluation way to separate disagreement caused by genuine item difficulty from disagreement caused by checklist ambiguity or shared confusion; both produce the same observed signal, but only the former distinguishes reliability, so the proposed evidence does not validly distinguish genuine gain from compliance under the problem's constraints.
